Les citoyens de Montréal-Nord ont eu l’o: Montréal-Nord residents had the chance to question three candidates directly at a public debate organized by their Table de quartier.
Une vingtaine de personnes ont assisté a: About twenty people attended the debate with three federal candidates at the Maison culturelle et communautaire de Montréal-Nord. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Montréal-Nord est un arrondissement où p: Montréal-Nord is a borough where structural challenges persist – housing, precarity, immigration, access to social services, and more. That is why we felt it was essential to cover the debate organized there by the Table de quartier, in which three federal candidates agreed to take part. La Converse, which received an invitation to attend, was the only media outlet present.
Au-delà des lignes de parti, le débat a: Beyond party lines, the debate made it possible to test political proposals against lived realities, in a neighbourhood whose local issues are often absent from the big election campaigns. We did note, however, that the audience was not as large as one might have hoped, and that it was made up mostly of members of the neighbourhood’s community organizations and activists. But this is partly explained by the limited promotion of the event, which was done only through the Table de quartier’s own channels.
L’absence des candidats du Parti conserv: The absence of the Conservative Party and Green Party candidates also highlighted the limits of this democratic exercise, since those in attendance could not hear their proposals or put questions to them.
<strong>À quelques jours d’un scrutin fé: A few days before a federal vote with an uncertain outcome, Montréal-Nord residents had a rare opportunity to question three candidates directly at a public debate organized by the Table de quartier. Housing, health, immigration, women’s rights – these were among the themes tackled over the course of a political evening fuelled by local realities. Our report.
Il est 18 h à la Maison culturelle et co: It is 6 p.m. at the Maison culturelle et communautaire de Montréal-Nord, and the mood is both studious and warm. While the Table de quartier team busies itself with last-minute preparations, people chat around the buffet. “I hope it will be interesting. I came to see what the candidates have to offer for our neighbourhood and for Montréal,” says Hélène, a resident who recently moved in a few streets away.
Peu après, les participants – une vingta: Shortly afterward, the participants – about twenty of them – take their seats in the room. Facing the audience, three candidates settle in: Jency Mercier for the Bloc Québécois, Abdelhaq Sari for the Liberal Party, and Catherine Gauvin for the New Democratic Party. Behind them, beyond the large bay windows, children play in the neighbouring park under the last rays of the day’s sunshine. It is a scene that contrasts with the political concerns of their elders inside.
Dans le public, on voit des citoyens att: In the audience there are attentive citizens and several local elected officials, but above all representatives of the neighbourhood’s community organizations. Everyone has come to hear what those seeking a seat in the House of Commons have to offer to address a reality too often marginalized in election campaigns: that of disadvantaged neighbourhoods.
« Il y a quelques semaines, notre consei: “A few weeks ago, our board of directors asked us if we could contribute to democracy by organizing this debate,” says the director of the Table de quartier before handing over to the moderator. The absence of the Conservative Party and the Green Party was noted – Conservative candidate Néhémie Dumay withdrew the day before, and the Green candidate, Émile Jetzer, never responded to the invitation extended to him.
Micherose Philosca lance alors le débat: Micherose Philosca then kicks off the debate with the first of nine themes selected by the Table de quartier. The principle is simple: each candidate has two minutes to present their proposals.
La question du coût de la vie prend rapi: The cost of living quickly takes centre stage. Asked about the tax measures being considered to support seniors, Jency Mercier says the Bloc Québécois wants to “increase old age pensions by 10% so that seniors don’t struggle to make ends meet.” A measure that would apply to all age groups and help put an end to what the candidate calls the “two-tier old age.”
Abdelhaq Sari, de son côté, rappelle les: Abdelhaq Sari, for his part, recalls the measures the Liberals have proposed to ease the effects of inflation, citing “a lower tax rate for low incomes” and the continuation of the Guaranteed Income Supplement. The city councillor stresses the need for a “strong government able to address the root causes of this crisis,” such as the trade war.
Abdelhaq Sari, candidat du Parti Libéral: Abdelhaq Sari, Liberal Party candidate. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Catherine Gauvin fait quant à elle valoi: Catherine Gauvin, for her part, argues that the NDP was there “during the pandemic to defend workers, seniors and vulnerable people,” saying these values of solidarity are “in the party’s DNA.” The left-wing party plans to raise taxes on the wealthiest in order to ease the tax burden on lower-income households.

Jency Mercier, la candidate du Bloc qui: Jency Mercier, the Bloc candidate who lives in Verdun, argues for greater provincial autonomy in housing management. “The Bloc wants federal funds to be transferred to Quebec without conditions,” she says, deploring the fact that some buildings are left to decay and stand empty, “with boards on the windows.” In her view, part of the rental market must be “taken out of the capitalist system,” and the transfer of federal land at low cost should be made easier.
Jency Mercier, candidate du Bloc Québéco: Jency Mercier, Bloc Québécois candidate. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Pour Abdelhaq Sari, candidat libéral et: For Abdelhaq Sari, the Liberal candidate and a Montréal-Nord city councillor since 2017, the response must be adapted to the local context. “You can’t have a one-size-fits-all approach for all of Canada. Realities differ from one neighbourhood to the next,” he explains, adding that the priority should be “increasing the supply of affordable housing” where needs are most pressing. He says the Liberal Party has a $25-billion plan for housing. However, after fact-checking, that amount is actually earmarked for “financing for innovative prefabricated home builders in Canada” and not for affordable housing.
De son côté, la candidate néo-démocrate: The NDP candidate, for her part, recalls her own childhood in a single-parent family. “The price of rent is appalling. My mother is in a co-op and it saved her,” says Catherine Gauvin. The NDP promises to create 120,000 social housing units, to regulate rents, to fight renovictions, and to use federal land exclusively for community or co-operative social housing projects.
En deux minutes, les candidats n’ont pas: In two minutes, the candidates don’t have time to say more, but the subject of housing will come up several times over the evening, notably when immigration is discussed.
L’augmentation du nombre de demandeurs d: The increase in the number of asylum seekers coming from the United States to flee the deportations promised by the Trump administration is one of the topics that has dominated the election campaign the most. Unsurprisingly, the management of immigration therefore prompts lively exchanges this Wednesday evening.
« L’un des rares centres d’hébergement p: “One of the few shelters for asylum seekers has to close for lack of funding. How does the federal government intend to support Quebec in welcoming asylum seekers with dignity?” asks the moderator. Montréal-Nord welcomes many newcomers, while the community organizations that help them struggle to survive every year.
Pour M. Sari, qui a souligné qu’il était: For Mr. Sari, who pointed out that he himself is an immigrant who arrived from Morocco in 2002, it is a matter of dignity. “Immigration is not a one-off event. It’s not only about welcoming people, but also about having the capacity to welcome them with dignity. However, once a person is on the territory, it’s our organizations, our cities, the provinces that will take charge of them, so we all have to work together.” He calls for stable, long-term funding for support organizations and shorter processing times for asylum claims.
Catherine Gauvin annonce alors que les n: Catherine Gauvin then announces that the New Democrats are committed to transferring $100 million from the federal government to the province to support it in welcoming immigrants, by funding organizations for their mission rather than by project. “We have to stop sprinkling funding envelopes around,” says the candidate.
Catherine Gauvin, candidate du Nouveau P: Catherine Gauvin, New Democratic Party candidate. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Sans surprise, les candidats restent dan: Unsurprisingly, the candidates stick to their respective party lines and sometimes struggle to tie their answers to the particular situation of Montréal-Nord. An observation that prompts the audience to make the most of the question period that followed.
Après que plusieurs autres thématiques c: After several other themes, such as violence against women, youth and health, have been addressed, audience members are invited to put their questions to the three candidates. Local concerns are at the heart of residents’ questions.
Interrogés sur leurs priorités pour la c: Asked about their priorities for the riding of Bourassa, all three candidates converge on housing. Abdelhaq Sari adds welcoming immigrants and supporting seniors to his priorities. Catherine Gauvin, for her part, cites the environment and health.
Plusieurs membres d’organismes communaut: With several members of community organizations in the audience, the question of funding for their organizations is quite naturally raised, using the example of the cut to grants for organizations specializing in employability. The Bloc candidate, like the New Democrat, commits to restoring these funds and to establishing stable, long-term funding for community organizations. The Liberal candidate argues for sustainable, structural funding.
Mais les réponses des candidats, qui ont: But the answers from the candidates, who deserve credit for taking part, unlike their Green Party and Conservative Party counterparts, are not always convincing. “I asked when they’re actually going to build their social housing! Because we always get nice speeches, but nothing concrete,” says Sylvie, a 61-year-old Montréal-Nord resident. The retiree denounces promises that come back every election and are never carried out: “All this time, they know we have housing problems, but they haven’t built anything in years, and we’re still waiting!”
Pour Sylvie, ce débat n’aura pas d’influ: For Sylvie, this debate will have no influence on her when she slips her ballot into the box: the sixty-something already knows who she will vote for, “along family lines.” Like her, many came mainly to support one of the candidates.
Au sujet de l’abstention des jeunes, qui: On the abstention of young people, who make up 15% of the population of Montréal-Nord, the candidates try to persuade. “You shouldn’t vote for a party, or for a person, but for your future. If you don’t take care of politics, it will take care of you,” says Abdelhaq Sari, with a knack for a catchy line that draws applause. The NDP proposes to cap internet subscription rates and limit interest rates on student loans, a commitment met with a few laughs in the room, proof that the proposal did not fully convince, even though the candidate is the only one to have made concrete proposals for young people.
Exercice démocratique difficile, mais né: A difficult but necessary democratic exercise, this meeting between residents and candidates ran up somewhat against the reality of federal elections, which deal with global rather than local issues. The debate nevertheless brought to light distinct visions in response to shared concerns.
À Montréal-Nord, les enjeux sont concret: In Montréal-Nord, the issues are concrete, urgent and at the heart of residents’ daily lives. Here, citizens expect less rhetoric than tangible commitments – a challenge. The candidates will know whether they have met it when they learn the election results on Monday evening.
Le débat se déplace ensuite sur la crise: The debate then shifts to the housing crisis, a burning issue in this borough where more than 35% of households live below the poverty line. M<sup>s</sup> Philosca also points out that Montréal-Nord has a vacancy rate of barely 0.4%, and that this housing shortage is driving rents up, while 71.6% of households are renters.
M<sup>me</sup> Mercier, de son côté, évo: M<sup>s</sup> Mercier, for her part, raises the issue of overstretched services and stresses the need to “respect our capacity to welcome people.” She believes that “Quebec has taken in a lot of people recently, without always having the means to do it properly.” She adds that the Bloc is demanding unconditional transfers so that Quebec’s autonomy is respected.
